steps.label: KP15 Convergence guarantees for overparameterized networks
Over-parameterization · 1/6
steps.speakerNotes: Over-parameterization means more parameters than data. The simplest example is least squares for a linear model.

steps.label: Over-parameterization · 1/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The loss is one half the squared norm of prediction minus label.

steps.label: Over-parameterization · 1/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: The equation has p unknowns but only n constraints,

steps.label: Over-parameterization · 1/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: the equation Xw=y p unknowns, n constraints

steps.label: Over-parameterization · 1/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: so the zero-loss solutions have p minus n degrees of freedom: not a point but a whole family.

steps.label: Over-parameterization · 1/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: Gradient descent gets zero training loss once it enters the family, yet the points in it differ on test data.

steps.label: The start decides · 2/6
steps.speakerNotes: In least squares GD converges to the starting point plus the smallest correction that fills the residual. With one sample the zero-loss solutions form a line.

steps.label: The start decides · 2/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: From the origin it converges to 0.6, 1.2 with test loss 0.2. From 2, 0 it converges to 2.2, 0.4 with test loss 1.8.

steps.label: The start decides · 2/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: A: (0.6,\,1.2) B: (2.2,\,0.4) one sample x=(1,2), y=3; grey: starts, dots: where GD converges A: w_0=(0,0) w_\infty=(0.6,\,1.2) test loss 0.2 B: w_0=(2,0) w_\infty=(2.2,\,0.4) test loss 1.8

steps.label: The start decides · 2/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: Both solutions have training loss zero while the test loss differs 9 times. Starting from zero gives the minimum-norm solution.

steps.label: Shallow quadratic network · 3/6
steps.speakerNotes: Least squares is convex, so guarantees are easy. Neural networks are non-convex and the worry is that GD sticks where the gradient is zero but the loss is high. The smallest non-convex network has one hidden layer and quadratic activation.

steps.label: Shallow quadratic network · 3/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: The source's conditions: width at least twice the input dimension, with fixed output weights having at least that many positive and negative ones.

steps.label: Shallow quadratic network · 3/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Three conclusions: every local minimum is global; every saddle has a negative-curvature direction; the global minimum loss is zero when the sample count is in range.

steps.label: Shallow quadratic network · 3/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: The note ran a small experiment: width 1 gives 0 percent, 2 gives 83, 4 gives 99, 8 gives 96.

steps.label: Shallow quadratic network · 3/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: the note's 100 runs (d=2, n=3): fraction reaching zero loss width k reaches zero 1 0% 2 83% 4 99% 8 96%

steps.label: Shallow quadratic network · 3/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: At width 1 no zero-loss solution exists. When the conditions fail the theorem says nothing.

steps.label: Deep ReLU · 4/6
steps.speakerNotes: The second result covers fully connected ReLU networks of l layers of width m with mean squared loss. Three kinds of conditions. First, data: each input has norm 1 and any two distinct samples are at least delta apart.

steps.label: Deep ReLU · 4/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: Second, initialization is Gaussian random.

steps.label: Deep ReLU · 4/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: Third, the width is large enough and the step small enough.

steps.label: Deep ReLU · 4/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: width and step wide enough, small enough step

steps.label: Deep ReLU · 4/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: The conclusion: the steps needed are about a polynomial in n and l, times one over delta squared, times the log of one over epsilon.

steps.label: Deep ReLU · 4/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: Three readings: the steps are polynomial, not exponential; epsilon sits in a log so each tenfold shrink costs a fixed extra number; small delta means many steps, close data slow it down.

steps.label: A conditional conclusion · 5/6
steps.speakerNotes: Put the two results side by side: both say that if the width is enough, the initialization random, the data separable and the step small,

steps.label: A conditional conclusion · 5/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: then the training loss can be made arbitrarily small.

steps.label: A conditional conclusion · 5/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: then the training loss can be made arbitrarily small

steps.label: A conditional conclusion · 5/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: This is a conditional conclusion: when the conditions fail it says nothing.

steps.label: A conditional conclusion · 5/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: More importantly, both results guarantee the training loss. Solutions with equal zero training loss can differ a lot on test loss.

steps.label: A conditional conclusion · 5/6 (5)
steps.speakerNotes: So optimization succeeding does not imply the model predicts well; that gap is what KP16 handles.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6
steps.speakerNotes: Finally, the common myths and the question left for the next unit.

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (1)
steps.speakerNotes: “an over-parameterized network must overfit”. optimization and generalization are separate; test generalization separately

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (2)
steps.speakerNotes: “a convergence guarantee is a generalization guarantee”. it guarantees training loss; test performance is not in the theorem

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (3)
steps.speakerNotes: “the steps are $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ so it is surely fast”. the constant has $\mathrm{poly}(n,l)$ and $1/\delta^2$, large for close data

steps.label: Myths and next question · 6/6 (4)
steps.speakerNotes: Solutions with the same zero training loss can differ a lot on test data. What decides generalization?
